extracted.intended_audience: USPTO patent examiners and patent applicants/attorneys
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for determining when subject matter is disqualified as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) (CREATE Act) — establishing common ownership or a qualifying joint research agreement, what evidence suffices, examiner procedures, timing/filing rules, and related double-patenting treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common ownership requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Actual ownership of the subject matter and the claimed invention by the same individual(s) or organization(s) or a legal obligation to assign both the subject matter and the claimed invention to the same individual(s) or organization(s)/business entity(ies) must be in existence at the time the claimed invention was made in order for the subject matter to be disqualified as prior art. A moral or unenforceable obligation would not evidence common ownership.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes illustrative examples (parent/subsidiary percentages, joint ventures, licenses). License to another does not necessarily make subject matter prior art if same person owned subject matter and invention at the time the invention was made. Common ownership is determined on the facts; an invention is 'made' when conception is complete (Pfaff v. Wells; Mergenthaler v. Scudder; In re Tansel). Common ownership at time of invention may be established irrespective of where invention was made (domestic or abroad).

rubrics_metrics.name: Applicant admission and 103(c) interaction
rubrics_metrics.description: An applicant’s admission that subject matter was developed prior to applicant’s invention would not make the subject matter prior art to applicant if the subject matter qualifies as prior art only under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f), or (g), and if the subject matter and the claimed invention were commonly owned at the time the invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If subject matter and invention were not commonly owned, an admission that the subject matter is prior art would be usable under 35 U.S.C. 103. See In re Fout for an example where an applicant's admission was used as prior art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Burden of proof for disqualification under 35 U.S.C. 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: The burden of establishing that subject matter is disqualified as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) is intended to be placed and reside upon the person or persons urging that the subject matter is disqualified (e.g., the patent applicant or patentee).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The burden should not be placed upon the patent examiner or the defendant in litigation because evidence of common ownership at the time the invention was made might not be available to them, whereas it should be readily available to applicant/patentee.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of double patenting rejections among commonly owned applications
rubrics_metrics.description: In appropriate circumstances, claims in commonly owned applications of different inventive entities may be rejected on the grounds of double patenting; such rejections can be overcome in appropriate circumstances by the filing of terminal disclaimers.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This practice prevents extending patent protection improperly while permitting legitimate benefits to inventors/assignees. Double patenting rejections may arise as a result of CREATE Act amendments and are authorized by case law (e.g., In re Bowers). See MPEP § 804 for guidance; terminal disclaimer per 37 CFR 1.321(d) can obviate double patenting rejections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficient statement to establish common ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Applications and references will be considered by the examiner to be owned by, or subject to an obligation of assignment to, the same person, at the time the invention was made, if the applicant(s) or an attorney or agent of record makes a statement to the effect that the application and the reference were, at the time the invention was made, owned by, or subject to an obligation of assignment to, the same person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The applicant/representative's statement is sufficient because of their obligation of candor and good faith. The statement should be clear and conspicuous (e.g., on separate paper or in a separately labeled section). Example provided: 'Application X and Patent A were, at the time the invention of Application X was made, owned by Company Z.' This statement alone is sufficient unless the examiner has independent evidence raising material doubt.

rubrics_metrics.name: Objective evidence examiners may require when material doubt exists
rubrics_metrics.description: If the examiner has independent evidence that raises a material doubt as to the accuracy of applicant’s representation of common ownership or obligation to assign, the examiner may explain the doubt and require objective evidence of common ownership or assignment as of the date of invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples of objective evidence that may be required: (A) reference to assignments recorded in USPTO (37 CFR Part 3) conveying entire rights to same person; (B) copies of unrecorded assignments filed in each application; (C) affidavit or declaration by common owner explaining facts supporting common ownership (signed by corporate official empowered to act); (D) other evidence establishing common ownership.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and timing requirement for a joint research agreement (JRA)
rubrics_metrics.description: 35 U.S.C. 103(c)(3) defines a 'joint research agreement' as a written contract, grant, or cooperative agreement entered into by two or more persons or entities for the performance of experimental, developmental, or research work in the field of the claimed invention, that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The JRA must be shown to be in effect on or before the time the later invention was made. The JRA may pre-date the CREATE Act effective date and is not required to be in effect on or before the prior art date of the reference sought to be disqualified.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substantive requirements to invoke CREATE Act safe harbor via JRA
rubrics_metrics.description: To overcome a 35 U.S.C. 103(a) rejection based upon subject matter that qualifies as prior art only under 102(e),(f) or (g) via the CREATE Act, the applicant must: (1) provide a statement that the prior art and the claimed invention were made by or on behalf of parties to a JRA that was in effect on or before the date the claimed invention was made; and (2) state that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the JRA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The applicant must comply with statute and rules. The application must disclose or be amended to disclose the names of the parties to the JRA (37 CFR 1.71(g)(1)). The statement should be on or begin on a separate sheet and must not be directed to other matters (37 CFR 1.4(c)), and must be signed per 37 CFR 1.33(b). If the examiner disqualifies subject matter under 103(c), the examiner will treat the application and the 102(e)/(f)/(g) prior art as if commonly owned for purposes of 103(a).

rubrics_metrics.name: 37 CFR 1.71(g) — amendment to disclose JRA parties: timing, fees, and effect
rubrics_metrics.description: An amendment disclosing the names of the parties to a JRA must be accompanied by the processing fee set forth in 37 CFR 1.17(i) if not filed within one of specified time periods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Permitted time periods: (i) within 3 months of filing date of a national application; (ii) within 3 months of entry of national stage (37 CFR 1.491); (iii) before mailing of first Office action on the merits; (iv) before mailing of first OA after filing an RCE (37 CFR 1.114). If filed after issue fee paid, the issued patent may not include JRA party names; correction then requires certificate of correction under 35 U.S.C. 255 and 37 CFR 1.323. Submission is subject to normal practice rules (37 CFR 1.116, 1.121, 1.312). Filing such an amendment while under final rejection may necessitate terminal disclaimer entry and reopening prosecution; examiner may refuse entry if not accompanied by appropriate terminal disclaimer (37 CFR 1.321(d)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Scope requirement for JRA safe harbor (activities within scope)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if a JRA existed prior to the later invention, the claimed invention must have been made as a result of activities undertaken within the scope of the JRA to qualify for disqualification of the prior art under 103(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Illustrative examples: (a) JRA effective after later invention — cannot invoke 103(c); (b) JRA in effect but limited to different activities/subject matter — cannot invoke 103(c) for inventions outside scope.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conditions required for a reference to be disqualified under 103(c)
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference used in an anticipatory rejection under 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f), or (g) is not disqualified as prior art unless: (A) proper evidence is filed; (B) the reference only qualifies as prior art under 102(e), (f) or (g) (i.e., not under 102(a) or (b)); and (C) the reference was used in an obviousness rejection under 35 U.S.C. 103(a).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examiners should recognize that a reference is generally only disqualified when all three conditions are met. See MPEP § 706.02(l)(3) for procedure.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure when application file has not established disqualification
rubrics_metrics.description: If the application file being examined has not established that the reference is disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c), the examiner will: (A) assume the reference is not disqualified under 103(c); (B) examine the application on all grounds other than any conflict between the reference patent(s)/application(s) arising from a possible 35 U.S.C. 103 rejection based on prior art under 102(e),(f),(g); (C) consider applicability of references under 103 including provisional rejections based on provisional prior art under 102(e); and (D) apply the best references against the claimed invention by rejections under 102 and 103 until such time the reference is disqualified under 103(c).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When applying references that qualify under 102(e) in a 103 rejection, the examiner should anticipate that the reference may later be disqualified under 103(c). If a statement of common ownership or assignment is filed in reply to a 103 rejection and claims are not amended, the examiner may not make the next Office action final if a new rejection is made (see MPEP §706.07(a)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examiner procedure when common ownership or JRA has been established
rubrics_metrics.description: If the application being examined has established that the reference is disqualified as prior art under 35 U.S.C. 103(c), the examiner will: (A) examine the applications as to all grounds, except 35 U.S.C. 102(e), (f) and (g) as they apply through 103; (B) examine the applications for double patenting (statutory and nonstatutory) and make a provisional rejection if appropriate; and (C) invite the applicant to file a terminal disclaimer to overcome any provisional or actual nonstatutory double patenting rejection, if appropriate (37 CFR 1.321).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a reference is disqualified under 103(c), it will be treated as commonly owned for double patenting analysis, which may give rise to double patenting rejections even between different inventive entities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Double patenting treatment where 103(c) disqualifies reference
rubrics_metrics.description: For double patenting analysis, the application or patent and the subject matter disqualified under 35 U.S.C. 103(c) as amended by the CREATE Act will be treated as if commonly owned. A double patenting rejection based on a non-commonly owned patent (treated as commonly owned pursuant to CREATE) may be obviated by filing a terminal disclaimer in accordance with 37 CFR 1.321(d).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Double patenting rejections prevent an organization from obtaining multiple patents with different expiration dates covering nearly identical subject matter. Terminal disclaimers should include provision that the later patent is enforceable only while commonly owned with the patent forming the basis for the rejection. See MPEP § 804 and § 804.02.

rubrics_metrics.name: Form paragraphs and examiner use for 35 U.S.C. 103 rejections
rubrics_metrics.description: MPEP provides form paragraphs (e.g., ¶ 7.20 statement of statutory basis 35 U.S.C. 103(a); ¶ 7.20.01, 7.20.02, 7.20.04) to be used in making appropriate rejections under 35 U.S.C. 103.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ¶ 7.20 quotes 35 U.S.C. 103(a) and has examiner notes about when to cite the statute (first actions on merits and final rejections). ¶ 7.20.01 should be used where applicant provided evidence of common ownership but the reference additionally qualifies under another subsection of 102. ¶ 7.20.02 addresses joint inventors and presumption of common ownership. ¶ 7.20.04 addresses attempts to disqualify under the common ownership/assignment provision but failing to provide a conspicuous statement; instructs applicant to file required evidence and suggests alternative overcoming routes (37 CFR 1.132 derivation or antedating under 1.131). Examiners must follow the form paragraph instructions and include bracketed reference identifiers where indicated.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content and placement requirements for the required JRA/ownership statement
rubrics_metrics.description: The statement to invoke the prior art disqualification under CREATE must state that the prior art and the claimed invention were made by or on behalf of parties to a JRA that was in effect on or before the claimed invention date, and that the claimed invention was made as a result of activities within the scope of the JRA. The statement should either be on or begin on a separate sheet and must not be directed to other matters (37 CFR 1.4(c)).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statement must be signed in accordance with 37 CFR 1.33(b). If the statement is filed in accordance with 103(c) and rules, the examiner will treat the application and the 102(e)/(f)/(g) prior art as commonly owned for 103(a) purposes. Submission remains subject to the rules of practice (37 CFR 1.116, 1.121, 1.312). If an amendment under 1.71(g) is used to disclose JRA parties to invoke safe harbor, timing and fee rules apply (see 1.71(g)(2)).

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples illustrating borderline ownership and JRA fact patterns
rubrics_metrics.description: The guidance includes multiple illustrative examples (e.g., parent owns 100% subsidiaries; parent owns 100% and 90% — not commonly owned; licensees; government inventors retaining rights; joint venture employees assigned to JV; spin-offs transferring application ownership; percent ownership mixes resulting in common ownership; JRAs going into effect after the later invention; JRAs limited in scope).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these examples to apply factual tests: determine ownership at time invention was made; determine whether license/assignment/obligation chain legally establishes obligation to assign to joint venture; verify JRA effective date and scope to decide whether 103(c) safe harbor applies.
